# Global Navigation and GNSS Measurements

Until now, most of our examples have lived in a friendly local world: a flat
plane, a fixed Cartesian reference frame, and distances small enough that Earth's
curvature is not the dominant problem. That approximation is useful. It is also
limited.

For global navigation, the vehicle moves over a rotating, curved Earth. A local
flat frame can still be useful, but only as a frame attached to a particular
location. If the vehicle moves far enough, the meaning of north, east, and down
changes with position. Gravity changes with latitude and height. The Earth rotates
under inertial space. A navigation algorithm that ignores those facts will slowly
turn geometry into error and then act surprised when the map does not forgive it.

This chapter introduces the external measurements that will bound that drift:
satellite radio navigation from a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS). We
will treat the GNSS receiver mostly as a black box that outputs timestamped
position, velocity, and uncertainty. That is enough for loosely coupled INS/GNSS
integration, which is the architecture used in the project.

The signal-processing and receiver-design details are important, but they are not
the focus here. Our goal is to understand what a GNSS receiver is estimating, why
it needs multiple satellites, why its errors are not simple Gaussian dust, and how
its position and velocity outputs become measurements in an INS/GNSS filter.

## From Local Coordinates to Global Coordinates

The flat-Earth approximation assumes that a local navigation frame can be treated
as fixed over the region of interest. For indoor robots, small drones, and many
short-range experiments, this is usually acceptable. For aircraft, ships, long-range
ground vehicles, and strategic navigation, it is not.

Global navigation commonly uses three frame ideas:

- **Earth-centered inertial (ECI)**: centered at Earth, but not rotating with
  Earth. This is the cleanest frame for Newtonian inertial dynamics.
- **Earth-centered Earth-fixed (ECEF)**: centered at Earth and rotating with
  Earth. Coordinates are fixed to the planet, so a point on Earth's surface has
  nearly constant ECEF coordinates.
- **Local navigation frame**: a tangent frame attached to the vehicle or a local
  reference point. In this course we usually use North-East-Down (NED), where
  position is represented by latitude, longitude, and height, and velocity is
  resolved into north, east, and down components.

The body frame is attached to the vehicle. The IMU measures angular rate and
specific force in this body frame. The navigation algorithm must transform those
measurements into the navigation frame, integrate the state, and keep track of the
fact that the navigation frame itself moves and rotates as the vehicle moves over
the ellipsoid.

The WGS84 ellipsoid gives the standard geometric model used by GPS and most
modern navigation systems. A geodetic position is normally written as latitude
$\phi$, longitude $\lambda$, and height $h$ above the ellipsoid. Latitude and
longitude are angular coordinates, not meters, so changes in latitude and longitude
must be scaled by the local radii of curvature before they behave like distances.

That detail matters in software. A filter state may store position errors in meters
while the nominal state stores latitude and longitude in radians. Mixing those
without an explicit conversion is a good way to create a bug that looks like a
physics problem.

## What GNSS Provides

GNSS is the generic term for satellite navigation constellations such as GPS,
Galileo, GLONASS, and BeiDou. A receiver estimates its position and clock offset
by listening to radio signals transmitted by satellites whose positions and clock
corrections are known from the broadcast navigation message.

At a high level, each satellite transmits:

- a time-tagged ranging signal;
- satellite orbit information, often called ephemeris;
- satellite clock correction information;
- additional navigation data used by the receiver.

The receiver compares the received signal timing against its own clock. If the
satellite clock and receiver clock were perfectly synchronized, signal travel time
would give range directly:

$$
\rho = c(t_r - t_s),
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light, $t_s$ is the transmit time, and $t_r$ is the receive
time.

The receiver clock is not perfect, so the measured quantity is a **pseudorange**:

$$
\tilde{\rho}_s =
\left\|\mathbf{r}_u - \mathbf{r}_s\right\|
+ c\,\delta t_u
- c\,\delta t_s
+ \epsilon_s.
$$

Here $\mathbf{r}_u$ is the receiver antenna position, $\mathbf{r}_s$ is the satellite
position, $\delta t_u$ is the receiver clock offset, $\delta t_s$ is the satellite clock
offset, and $\epsilon_s$ collects unmodeled errors such as atmospheric delay,
multipath, receiver noise, and residual orbit or clock error.

The receiver has four basic unknowns in a standard single-antenna position fix:
three position components and receiver clock offset. That is why a three-dimensional
GNSS solution needs at least four satellites. More satellites make the solution
overdetermined, which lets the receiver estimate a better solution and reject bad
measurements when the geometry and integrity checks support it.

::: {.callout-note title="Figure placeholder: GNSS pseudorange geometry"}
Add a diagram showing several satellites, the receiver antenna, true geometric
ranges, pseudorange spheres, and the receiver clock-bias term that shifts all ranges.
:::

GNSS can also estimate velocity. A receiver often uses carrier Doppler or
pseudorange-rate measurements to estimate range rate to each satellite. These range
rates constrain the receiver velocity and receiver clock drift. For our loosely
coupled treatment, the receiver output is simply:

$$
\mathbf{z}_{GNSS,k}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{p}_{GNSS,k} \\
\mathbf{v}_{GNSS,k}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

with a timestamp and some statement of uncertainty. The receiver may report that
uncertainty as a covariance matrix, horizontal and vertical accuracy estimates, a
dilution-of-precision value, or a vendor-specific quality flag. In real projects, the
exact receiver interface matters. In this course, we will model it as a position and
velocity measurement with covariance $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS,k}$.

## GNSS Error Sources

GNSS is an external reference, but it is not truth. A receiver solution is an estimate
from radio measurements, and radio measurements are sensitive to the environment.

Common GNSS error sources include:

- **Satellite geometry**: if all visible satellites are clustered in the same part of
  the sky, the position solution is weak in some directions.
- **Atmospheric propagation**: ionospheric and tropospheric delays change the
  apparent signal travel time.
- **Multipath**: signals can reflect off buildings, water, terrain, or vehicle
  structure before reaching the antenna.
- **Non-line-of-sight reception**: the direct signal may be blocked, leaving only a
  reflected signal.
- **Receiver noise and tracking limits**: weak signals, low carrier-to-noise ratio,
  and high dynamics can degrade the measurement.
- **Outages and obstruction**: tunnels, indoor spaces, dense urban corridors,
  foliage, and vehicle body masking can remove satellites from view.
- **Interference and jamming**: GNSS signals are weak by the time they reach the
  receiver, so interference can deny or corrupt measurements.
- **Timing and synchronization error**: a GNSS measurement must be compared
  against the INS state at the same time of validity.

These errors are not all independent, zero-mean, or white. Multipath can be
time-correlated. Receiver filtering can smooth noise but increase its correlation
time. Satellite geometry changes slowly. A high-rate GNSS output does not
automatically mean that every sample contains independent information.

That point matters for Kalman filtering. If $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ is too small, the
filter will believe GNSS too aggressively and may inject jumps or multipath errors
into the inertial solution. If $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ is too large, the filter will fail to
correct INS drift quickly enough. A practical implementation should adapt or gate
GNSS measurements using receiver quality flags, innovation size, reported accuracy,
satellite count, geometry, and knowledge of the operating environment.

## Why INS and GNSS Fit Together

An inertial navigation system and a GNSS receiver fail in different ways. That is
why they are useful together.

| Sensor | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| INS / IMU | high-rate, smooth, self-contained short-term motion | drifts over time because biases and noise are integrated |
| GNSS | globally referenced position and velocity | lower rate, noisier short term, vulnerable to obstruction and interference |

INS gives the filter a high-rate propagation model. GNSS gives the filter an
external correction. During a short GNSS outage, the INS can coast. When GNSS
returns, it can pull the inertial solution back toward the global reference frame.
The system is not magic; it is a trade between short-term continuity and long-term
bounded error.

## Loosely Coupled INS/GNSS Integration

In a loosely coupled architecture, the GNSS receiver computes its own navigation
solution first. The INS/GNSS filter then uses that receiver solution as a measurement.
The filter does not process raw satellite pseudoranges or carrier-phase observables.

This is the architecture we will use:

1. The IMU drives high-rate strapdown propagation.
2. The GNSS receiver outputs timestamped position and velocity.
3. The filter forms a GNSS-minus-INS innovation.
4. The Kalman update estimates the INS error state.
5. The estimated error is injected back into the nominal navigation state.

::: {.callout-note title="Figure placeholder: loosely coupled INS/GNSS architecture"}
Add a block diagram showing raw IMU measurements feeding strapdown propagation,
GNSS position/velocity feeding the measurement update, and estimated error-state
corrections being injected into the nominal INS state.
:::

The nominal inertial state may be represented as

$$
\mathbf{x}_{nom}
=
\left[
\mathbf{p},
\mathbf{v},
\mathbf{q},
\mathbf{b}_a,
\mathbf{b}_g
\right],
$$

where $\mathbf{p}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, $\mathbf{q}$ is attitude,
$\mathbf{b}_a$ is accelerometer bias, and $\mathbf{b}_g$ is gyroscope bias. The
error-state filter estimates small corrections:

$$
\delta \mathbf{x}
=
\left[
\delta \mathbf{p},
\delta \mathbf{v},
\delta \boldsymbol{\theta},
\delta \mathbf{b}_a,
\delta \mathbf{b}_g
\right]^T.
$$

For a basic loose position and velocity update, the measurement innovation is

$$
\mathbf{y}_k
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{p}_{GNSS,k} - \mathbf{p}_{INS,k} \\
\mathbf{v}_{GNSS,k} - \mathbf{v}_{INS,k}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If the GNSS antenna is not located at the same physical point as the IMU, this
innovation must include a lever-arm correction. If $\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$ is the
known vector from the IMU origin to the GNSS antenna expressed in body axes,
then the antenna position is approximately

$$
\mathbf{p}_{ant}
=
\mathbf{p}_{INS}
+ \mathbf{C}_b^n \boldsymbol{\ell}^b,
$$

with an analogous velocity correction when angular motion of the lever arm is
significant. Do not ignore the lever arm just because it is inconvenient. On a small
ground robot it may be negligible. On an aircraft, ship, or high-dynamics vehicle,
it can be the difference between a clean innovation and a self-inflicted residual.

The simplest measurement matrix for a position and velocity update is

$$
\mathbf{H}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{I}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 \\
\mathbf{0}_3 & \mathbf{I}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Depending on sign convention, some texts write the innovation as INS-minus-GNSS
and use negative identity blocks instead. Either convention is fine if it is used
consistently. In this course, use GNSS-minus-INS for the innovation above.

```{python}
#| label: loose-gnss-update-interface
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
import numpy as np


def loose_gnss_update(error_state_mean, P, ins_position, ins_velocity,
                      gnss_position, gnss_velocity, R_gnss):
    """One loose INS/GNSS Kalman update for position and velocity."""
    innovation = np.concatenate([
        gnss_position - ins_position,
        gnss_velocity - ins_velocity,
    ])

    H = np.zeros((6, 15))
    H[0:3, 0:3] = np.eye(3)  # position error
    H[3:6, 3:6] = np.eye(3)  # velocity error

    S = H @ P @ H.T + R_gnss
    K = np.linalg.solve(S, H @ P).T

    delta_x = error_state_mean + K @ (innovation - H @ error_state_mean)

    I = np.eye(P.shape[0])
    P_updated = (I - K @ H) @ P @ (I - K @ H).T + K @ R_gnss @ K.T

    return delta_x, P_updated
```

The code above is not a complete INS/GNSS system. It is the measurement-update
shape. A complete implementation also needs strapdown propagation, error-state
propagation, measurement gating, timestamp handling, lever-arm compensation,
error injection, and error-state reset.

## Loose, Tight, and Deep Coupling

The coupling terms describe where GNSS information enters the integrated
navigation algorithm [@groves].

- **Loosely coupled**: use the GNSS receiver position and velocity solution.
  This is position-domain integration. It is straightforward and matches the
  project architecture.
- **Tightly coupled**: use raw or corrected satellite ranging measurements such
  as pseudorange and pseudorange rate. This is range-domain integration. It can
  keep using partial satellite information when a receiver-level position fix is
  unavailable, but it requires receiver measurements and more detailed models.
- **Deeply coupled**: integrate INS aiding directly with receiver tracking loops.
  This is receiver-design territory and is outside this course's implementation
  scope.

For this course, tight and deep coupling are comparison points only. They are worth
knowing because they explain why professional GNSS/INS systems can look more
complicated than the filter we implement here. They are not required for the
assignment.

## Practical Checklist for the Project

When using GNSS measurements in the INS/GNSS project, check the following:

- Confirm the coordinate frame of the GNSS position and velocity.
- Convert latitude and longitude errors to metric errors before filtering, or use
  an ECEF/local NED representation consistently.
- Use the GNSS timestamp, not the time at which your code happened to process the
  message.
- Account for the IMU-to-antenna lever arm when it is non-negligible.
- Gate large innovations before letting them update the filter.
- Choose $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ from reported uncertainty when available; otherwise
  choose conservative values and tune using innovation statistics.
- Treat outages explicitly. Do not feed stale GNSS measurements as if they were
  current.

The next chapter develops the curved-Earth strapdown equations used for INS
propagation. After that, the IMU error chapter explains why the error-state model
needs bias and noise states. Together, those pieces give us the loose INS/GNSS
